Discussion: On the real ~13.9%-prevalence CDC data, the plain baseline typically shows high accuracy but noticeably lower recall than on the balanced dataset — with genuine class imbalance and roughly 6x more negative than positive examples, the model can minimize loss by mostly predicting the majority (non-diabetic) class, quietly missing many true diabetic cases. Both class weighting (pos_weight) and SMOTE oversampling should meaningfully raise recall (catching more true diabetic cases) at some cost to precision (more false alarms), which is the correct trade-off direction for a screening tool per our Section 5.5 discussion. Class weighting is the cheaper technique (a one-line loss change, same training set size, no extra training time), while SMOTE synthesizes new minority-class examples and trains on a much larger, rebalanced training set, which can push recall even higher at a larger precision cost since it also changes the feature-space density the model trains on, not just the loss weighting. Because this is now the full 253,680-row original dataset rather than a scaled-down approximation, these results are directly comparable to published benchmarks on this dataset (e.g. the ~14%-prevalence numbers widely reported for this CDC BRFSS2015 data).

Stand-Out Suggestion 3: Feature Engineering¶

Let's test whether adding a small number of clinically-motivated interaction features — before any model training — improves performance more than hyperparameter tuning alone did. We'll engineer two interaction terms (BMI * Age, HighBP * HighChol) on the original balanced dataset, then retrain our best-performing configuration (Dropout + Weight Decay + LR Scheduling) on the engineered features and compare against the equivalent model trained on raw features only.

In [46]:
print("Feature engineering: creating interaction terms")
print("=" * 70)

df_fe = df.copy()
df_fe["BMI_x_Age"] = df_fe["BMI"] * df_fe["Age"]
df_fe["HighBP_x_HighChol"] = df_fe["HighBP"] * df_fe["HighChol"]

engineered_features = ["BMI_x_Age", "HighBP_x_HighChol"]
print(f"New features added: {engineered_features}")
print(df_fe[engineered_features + ["Diabetes_binary"]].corr()["Diabetes_binary"])

X_fe = df_fe.drop(columns=["Diabetes_binary"])
y_fe = df_fe["Diabetes_binary"]

X_fe_train, X_fe_temp, y_fe_train, y_fe_temp = train_test_split(
    X_fe, y_fe, test_size=0.4, random_state=RANDOM_SEED, stratify=y_fe
)
X_fe_val, X_fe_test, y_fe_val, y_fe_test = train_test_split(
    X_fe_temp, y_fe_temp, test_size=0.5, random_state=RANDOM_SEED, stratify=y_fe_temp
)

fe_scaler = StandardScaler()
X_fe_train_scaled = fe_scaler.fit_transform(X_fe_train)
X_fe_val_scaled = fe_scaler.transform(X_fe_val)
X_fe_test_scaled = fe_scaler.transform(X_fe_test)

fe_train_loader, fe_val_loader, fe_test_loader = make_loaders(
    X_fe_train_scaled, y_fe_train, X_fe_val_scaled, y_fe_val, X_fe_test_scaled, y_fe_test
)

print(f"\nEngineered feature set shape: {X_fe_train_scaled.shape[1]} features "
      f"(original 21 + {len(engineered_features)} engineered)")

print("Training best configuration (Dropout + Weight Decay + LR Scheduling) WITH engineered features")
print("=" * 70)

fe_model = DiabetesClassifierWithDropout(
    input_size=X_fe_train_scaled.shape[1], hidden_sizes=[64, 32, 16], dropout_prob=0.3
).to(device)
fe_criterion = nn.BCELoss()
fe_optimizer = optim.AdamW(fe_model.parameters(), lr=0.001, weight_decay=1e-4)
fe_scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(fe_optimizer, mode="min", factor=0.5, patience=5)

_, fe_train_losses, fe_val_losses = train_model_with_scheduler(
    model=fe_model, train_loader=fe_train_loader, val_loader=fe_val_loader,
    criterion=fe_criterion, optimizer=fe_optimizer, scheduler=fe_scheduler,
    device=device, num_epochs=100, print_every=25
)

fe_results = evaluate_model(fe_model, fe_test_loader, device)
print(f"\nWith engineered features -- Accuracy: {fe_results['accuracy']:.4f} | "
      f"Precision: {fe_results['precision']:.4f} | Recall: {fe_results['recall']:.4f} | "
      f"F1: {fe_results['f1']:.4f} | ROC-AUC: {fe_results['roc_auc']:.4f}")

track_experiment(
    name="FeatureEngineered (best config)", model=fe_model,
    train_losses=fe_train_losses, val_losses=fe_val_losses, test_results=fe_results,
    notes=f"Best config (Dropout+WeightDecay+LRSched) retrained with {engineered_features} interaction features added"
)

print("\nFeature engineering vs. best hyperparameter-tuned-only model (Combined, raw features):")
final_comparison = display_experiment_comparison()
final_comparison[final_comparison["Experiment"].isin(["Combined (Dropout+WeightDecay+LRSched)", "FeatureEngineered (best config)"])]

Discussion: Comparing the FeatureEngineered (best config) row to the Combined (Dropout+WeightDecay+LRSched) row (same hyperparameters, only the feature set differs) isolates the effect of feature engineering from the effect of hyperparameter tuning. If the engineered-feature model shows a further improvement in F1/ROC-AUC on top of the tuned baseline, that supports the note in Section 6.5 Part B that domain-informed feature engineering can rival or exceed further hyperparameter tuning — with the added benefit that interaction terms like HighBP * HighChol are also directly interpretable to a clinical audience, unlike a marginal architecture or learning-rate tweak.

Conclusion & Next Steps¶

Congratulations on completing this hands-on deep learning project! You’ve successfully applied neural network fundamentals to a structured data classification task, demonstrating not only technical competence but also an understanding of data preprocessing, model evaluation, and performance optimization.

The techniques and workflows you’ve built here extend far beyond this dataset. The same methods can be applied to credit risk assessment, customer churn prediction, quality control, and more challenges in other structured-data domains. To continue your deep learning journey, explore new datasets, experiment with model architectures, and iterate on performance and interpretability.
